forecasts.reference-class: UK immigration settlement policy reforms proposing a 10-year qualifying period for Indefinite Leave to Remain (earned settlement) as outlined in official consultations and policy briefs.

sources.claim: The Earned Settlement model would increase the standard qualifying period for settlement to ten years, with potential reductions based on contributions to the UK economy and society.
The white paper proposes changing the five-year settlement standard to ten years, with exemptions for some routes and a possible faster track for certain contributors.

The government’s consultation (open until February 12, 2026) would lengthen many routes to settlement toward a ten-year framework, with exemptions and potential adjustments for high earners or early access under certain conditions.
The Long Residence route already uses a 10-year qualifying period for settlement, counting time across various routes toward a 10-year threshold.
The default qualifying period for settlement will be increased from five to ten years; a time-adjustment model based on four pillars will determine improvements or delays.
Parliament's briefing notes that the government announced a ten-year baseline with exceptions; some groups may qualify earlier and others later, depending on circumstances.
Analysis indicates the standard waiting period would rise to 10 years with notable exemptions by skill level and visa route, and some routes retaining shorter periods.
Consultation on earned settlement closes February 12, 2026; changes could come into effect as soon as April 2026.

The government states that the new earned settlement model will increase the standard qualifying period for settlement to ten years, with the possibility of shorter or longer paths based on 'time adjustment' pillars (character, integration, contribution, residence).

The 2025 immigration white paper proposed increasing the permanent residence/settlement qualifying period from five to ten years, with some cases qualifying sooner; changes were described as pending implementation and possible to begin in April 2026.

causal-factors.rationale: GOV.UK documents explicitly set a 10-year baseline and a time-adjustment framework, indicating a substantial policy shift toward longer qualifying periods.

causal-factors.rationale: The consultation is active, runs for 12 weeks, and government signals potential changes commencing in 2026, sustaining momentum toward adoption by May 2026.

causal-factors.rationale: Nov 2025 government updates and press releases reiterate the move to a 10-year baseline with conditions; implementation could begin in 2026.

causal-factors.rationale: Rule changes require changes to immigration rules and possible parliamentary passage, which could delay full adoption beyond May 2026.

causal-factors.rationale: Carve-outs mean some groups may access settlement earlier, but the baseline move to 10 years remains in place for many routes.

causal-factors.name: Baseline 10-year standard for settlement under Earned Settlement (time-adjust pillars: Character, Integration, Contribution, Residence)
causal-factors.rationale: Official policy documents and public consultation indicate a shift from a five-year path to a ten-year baseline, with reductions possible through pillar-based time adjustments for high-contributors; this is the core signal behind the forecasted reform. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Public consultation closed Feb 12, 2026; changes expected from April 2026 (subject to consultation outcomes)
causal-factors.rationale: The government states the 10-year baseline as the default in the Earned Settlement consultation; the Home Office indicates changes to permanent residence rules are planned to begin in April 2026; momentum from the process suggests near-term adoption. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10267/))

causal-factors.name: Policy timetable uncertainty and risk of delay due to no overall timetable and need for rule changes
causal-factors.rationale: There is no single timetable for the white paper proposals to come into force; changes occur through immigration rules and depend on consultation outcomes, implying potential delays beyond May 2026. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10267/))

causal-factors.name: Complexity and patchwork exemptions by route (time-adjust pillars) creating ambiguity and implementation risk
causal-factors.rationale: The Earned Settlement framework includes multiple pillars and route-specific exemptions; while the baseline is 10 years, exemptions may accelerate or slow some paths and complicate rollout. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Legal/political risk: retrospective application and transitional arrangements; potential challenges or revisions post-consultation
causal-factors.rationale: The consultation process and subsequent debates raise the possibility of transitional arrangements or legal challenges that could alter the pace or shape of reforms. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10267/))

causal-factors.name: Budgetary and labour-market implications (fees, no recourse to public funds, and impact on employers), which could deter or slow adoption
causal-factors.rationale: Longer ILR timelines imply higher immigration costs and potential welfare restrictions; these fiscal and workforce considerations create pushback that could slow adoption. ([migrationobservatory.ox.ac.uk](https://migrationobservatory.ox.ac.uk/resources/commentaries/changes-to-settlement-what-do-they-mean/?utm_source=openai))

causal-factors.name: Policy signal to raise baseline to 10 years (Earned Settlement)
causal-factors.rationale: Gov.uk materials and the 2025 Earned Settlement consultation state a new baseline of 10 years for settlement with potential time adjustments, a direction echoed in Commons Library briefing as the policy path; this signal suggests the 10-year threshold could be in force by or shortly after April 2026. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Time-adjustment pillars and exemptions enabling earlier settlement for some groups
causal-factors.rationale: The earned settlement framework creates reductions from the 10-year baseline for high earners, public service roles, volunteering, and other criteria, meaning many applicants could reach settlement sooner than 10 years. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

causal-factors.name: Regulatory timetable suggesting changes could take effect from April 2026
causal-factors.rationale: Official sources indicate reforms could begin in April 2026, increasing the likelihood that some routes will implement the 10-year baseline by May 2026. ([commonslibrary.parliament.uk](https://commonslibrary.parliament.uk/research-briefings/cbp-10267/))

causal-factors.name: Consultation closure and ongoing uncertainty around transitional arrangements
causal-factors.rationale: The public consultation closed on February 12, 2026, and final decisions depend on rule changes and potential transitional protections, introducing uncertainty about universal adoption by May 2026. ([gov.uk](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/earned-settlement/a-fairer-pathway-to-settlement-statement-and-accompanying-consultation-on-earned-settlement-accessible))

synthesis: Policy momentum supports a 10-year baseline, but practical rollout risks temper the forecast. A calibrated probability around 70% captures both the direction and the timing uncertainty.
